doc.title: Mike Wofford interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 13, 1998

chapter: Making a living: studio and odd work
title: Craft versus art in studio playing and the late 60s decline of jazz
summary: Studio dates meant playing with superb musicians and writers like Dave Grusin; he took it partly for survival during jazz's late-60s slump.

story.theme_name: Jazz musicians in the movies and film scoring
story.community_name: Studio work and jingles: New York session life

blocks.x: Well you said a couple of minutes ago you were talking about the studio music and you said most of it was just craft. And at first I thought you were going to say crap. But I think it’s a telling thing that you didn’t say that, because even playing on a Rice-a-Roni commercial, you have to do what’s required, and not more. Because I’ve heard plenty of players who can play the piano like crazy but they don’t understand the gig — if it’s solo piano if it’s in a restaurant or something.

Yeah. And that’s where the professional, again, yeah you’re absolutely right. There’s craft and there’s art as far as I’m concerned. It’s kind of like the old line, years ago someone said, “There’s music and there’s the music business.” And they’re very often two very different things. Yeah. On any given day in a Hollywood studio, and it would be the same in New York, I was sitting with the greatest players in the world, guys who © Fillius Jazz Archive -15-

could sit in a symphony orchestra, who could do all kinds of stuff. So there was nothing demeaning or ridiculous about being there, I mean you were lucky to be there. But a lot of times the product you were going for was maybe — this, we’re not talking here Pierre Boulez, but on the other hand, in many cases it was wonderful music, great writers who took it very seriously, even if it was just fairly innocuous film, took the writing very seriously. I worked for Dave Grusin a lot. Dave Grusin wrote beautiful stuff for some comedy shows we used to do and the string writing and everything would be absolutely gorgeous. Tom Scott and some of those people.
You want me to pause for a second? Yes, tell him I’ll call him a little bit later. Ray Conniff is coming tomorrow.

Oh. You let me know your time frame too, it’s two o’clock. So anyway, yeah, you know studio work was just something that happened. And about that same time jazz went into another one of its declines, you know the late ‘60s, early ‘70s was a very difficult time for jazz. I mean there have been all these valleys over there, and that was one of them. And at the time it just seemed like again it was partly survival. There’s no point in starving. I mean you just do what you have to do. And if there’d been more interesting stuff going on to do I would have tried to do that. But at that particular point in my life it was good work, and I did learn a lot about it as a player and even as a writer. And I sat with some really wonderful players.
